Cela fait déjà un mois que l’attaque du: It has already been a month since the Hamas attack on Israeli territory. A month of relentless Israeli bombing of the Gaza Strip. La Converse spoke with Yacoub Awad*, a 34-year-old Palestinian refugee whose family is trapped in the hell of Gaza.
Il est 10 h 35. J’ai rendez-vous avec Ya: It’s 10:35 a.m. I’m meeting Yacoub Awad at the Van Houtte café near Université du Québec à Montréal. When I walk in, I find him in the line to the counter. Behind him, a young woman is watching a video on her phone about “Hamas using civilians as human shields.”
Une fois son café en main, le jeune homm: Coffee in hand, the young man joins me by the window. He is lost in thought. “These days, I don’t say I’m Palestinian anymore,” he confides with a smile, taking off his wool hat. “When people ask, I dare them to guess, but I just go along with whatever nationality they give me. Turkish? Of course. Moroccan? Why not! Pakistani? Certainly.”
Cela fait 23 mois, autant dire une étern: It has been 23 months, an eternity, since Yacoub last kissed his mother’s forehead and shared a knowing laugh with his father.
« Je n’ai pas entendu la voix de mon pap: “I haven’t heard my dad’s voice since October 13,” he says with a sigh. He opens WhatsApp to listen for the hundredth time to the last voice message from his father, who has been stuck in Gaza since the start of the war, along with his mom and three of his siblings.
« <em>Al Hamdoulillah</em>, tout va bien: “Al Hamdoulillah, everything is fine,” says the voice, from the heart of hell. “There’s no water, no electricity, no medicine, but Al Hamdoulillah. Be reassured, be reassured, be reassured, only what God has planned will happen. Peace be with you,” says the head of the Awad family, addressing his message to Yacoub and his other siblings who live in the United Arab Emirates.
L’enregistrement se termine, et Yacoub e: The recording ends, and Yacoub continues: “The hardest part, is this ‘Al Hamdoulillah.’ When I talk to my mother, it’s what she says too: ‘Al Hamdoulillah, we are alive.’ Oh, how I hate that, because I don’t know what it really means, what it hides,” he explains, since the expression is also used when going through a hard ordeal.
Le silence s’installe, troublé par la mu: Silence settles in, broken by the music and the hubbub of the café. “Honestly, I’m afraid to ask them too many questions. I tell myself that if they put their trust in God, it’s to stay strong.”
Depuis le 7 octobre, la situation à Gaza: Since October 7, the situation in Gaza has been getting worse, and <l1>the bombing continues day and night</l1>. <l2>Famine is part of daily life</l2>, and <l3>communications are cut off</l3>.
« C’est extrêmement difficile de les con: “It’s extremely hard to reach them. Three days ago, I couldn’t get through and I told myself: ‘That’s it, it’s happened. They’re dead. They killed them!’”
Au début du mois de novembre, la famille: At the beginning of November, Yacoub’s family picked up one of the Israeli leaflets dropped from planes, ordering them to evacuate because the neighbourhood was going to be bombed.
« Ils sont hébergés dans la maison de <e: “They’re staying in the house of jeddou, my grandfather, who took in the whole extended family. There are more than a hundred people in his home.” The house is in Gaza City, between Al-Shifa Hospital and the Al-Shati refugee camp.
« Mes grands-parents sont eux-mêmes des: “My grandparents are refugees themselves. They come from different parts of Palestine: Hiribya, Rafah, Safad and Majdal Bani Fadil. During the <l1>Nakba</l1> in 1948, they were forced to leave their land and their villages and settle in the Gaza Strip.”
Un voile de tristesse obscurcit le visag: A veil of sadness darkens Yacoub’s face. “In our culture, we have a lot of children, so we don’t disappear. But if this keeps up, they’re going to wipe them all out. It’s not just my parents, it’s also my uncles, my aunts, my cousins. Can you even conceive of losing an entire lineage, an entire family tree?” he says angrily.
Ce matin, Yacoub a réussi à parler avec: This morning, Yacoub managed to speak with his younger brother, who told him they had to split up. The cousins decided to stay, despite the threat. The oldest and most vulnerable left to take refuge at an uncle’s place, farther south.
« Habituellement, ma famille vit aux Émi: “My family normally lives in the United Arab Emirates. They were visiting Gaza when the war broke out. Since then, they’ve been waiting on the goodwill of the Egyptians to cross the Rafah border crossing.”
Devant cette situation, Yacoub dit avoir: Faced with this situation, Yacoub says he has developed an obsession: “I can’t put my phone down. I’m constantly checking for messages. I watch the videos of the dead and wounded that are circulating and I keep asking myself: ‘Is that my friend? My neighbour? My family? Are those ruins our house?’ I’m losing all my bearings, my landmarks are being erased, my people are dying, my memories are all I have left. I have no place left to return to, and I fear I’ll have no one left to return to.”
Le rire d’un enfant résonne dans le café: A child’s laughter rings out in the café on Sainte-Catherine Street. “In Gaza, every breath of life can be cut off at any minute. There’s the bombing, but there’s also this environment with no hygiene, where disease threatens to spread at an alarming speed. These are the conditions in which my compatriots live and risk dying.”

Yacoub est arrivé au Canada le 25 décemb: Yacoub arrived in Canada on December 25, 2021, via Roxham Road. He filed a refugee claim, which led, two years later, to protected person status. Because of administrative delays, the trip he had planned to take this fall to see his parents in Europe had to be postponed. That’s when his family decided to go on vacation in Gaza.
« Si seulement le gouvernement canadien: “If only the Canadian government had processed my claim as efficiently as it processed the claims of Ukrainian refugees…” says Yacoub, who carries the guilt of that missed reunion.
Entre deux gorgées de café, le jeune hom: Between sips of coffee, the young man recalls his father’s advice when the first bombs fell on Gaza: “Listen, my son! Think of yourself, focus on your future. And above all: be careful.”
« Je suis né aux Émirats et j’y ai résid: “I was born in the Emirates and have lived there all my life. But I will never get citizenship in that country, or all the rights that come with it,” he explains. Yacoub holds a passport issued by the Palestinian Authority, which means he needs a visa and has to endure lengthy bureaucratic hassles to travel, whatever the destination. “With my passport, I can’t go anywhere but Gaza,” he says, glancing out the window. “And in Gaza, you don’t live, you survive.”

En 2014, Yacoub était à Gaza lorsque la: In 2014, Yacoub was in Gaza when war broke out. It was the height of summer. “It lasted eight weeks. Bombs were falling all day long. You couldn’t afford to sleep, because you didn’t know if you would wake up alive,” he says curtly.
« Il y avait le bruit, la terre qui trem: “There was the noise, the ground shaking, the smoke, and that stench of burning and dust. This time it’s even harder, more devastating. The force of the bombing is much greater, and they’re hitting everywhere in the Gaza Strip.”
Yacoub ferme les yeux, son visage se rem: Yacoub closes his eyes, his face darkens, and he shakes his head: “My brother told me there’s an acrid smell in the air, coming from all the unburied bodies, the rotting flesh.”
Le Palestinien, qui a vécu neuf mois à G: The Palestinian man, who lived in Gaza for nine months in 2021, says his people’s living conditions have always been bad, even in times of relative peace. “We have always lived under the Israeli blockade, with its sporadic strikes, its air and naval military operations. We only had electricity eight hours a day. We had to wait to fill the water tanks, and few people have drinking water running from their taps (<l1>only 5%</l1> of residents). The majority of Gazans still live in total food insecurity (<l2>68%</l2>). Unemployment is very high (<l3>45%</l3>), because there are few opportunities to earn a living.”
L’exilé me montre un document qui lui a: The exile shows me a document he was given by the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).
« Ce papier démontre que nous avons été: “This paper shows that we were forced to leave our ancestral land and that we now live in Gaza. This paper certifies that we are refugees in our own country! What is Gaza, if not a refugee camp for hundreds of thousands of Palestinians, an open-air prison? And even then, I think prisoners are entitled to a kind of justice that Palestinians don’t have,” he says bitterly.
Yacoub se répète la phrase de l’intellec: Yacoub keeps repeating a line from Palestinian-American intellectual Edward Said: “<l1>We are the victims of victims, the refugees of refugees</l1>.”
Il pleut dehors. Un groupe d’étudiants u: It’s raining outside. A group of university students has just taken shelter in the café. Watching their closeness, Yacoub remembers the warmth of the people back home. “It’s true that life is hard in Gaza, but Gaza is also remarkable human beings.”
<strong>« Être Palestinien est une intif: “Being Palestinian is an intifada in itself”
Le café continue à se remplir. Certains: The café keeps filling up. Some customers are wearing keffiyehs. This reassures Yacoub, who brings up the November 4 demonstration, where thousands of people expressed their solidarity with the Palestinian cause: “It’s comforting to see the support of diverse communities, and to see Palestinian flags flying in the air along with signs denouncing the injustices we suffer.”
« D’un autre côté, on voit aussi comment: “On the other hand, we also see how Western governments support the Israeli state, by financing the war and refusing to call for a ceasefire.”
Yacoub poursuit sur un ton ferme : « Le: Yacoub continues in a firm tone: “Refusing to denounce war crimes, a genocide, the will to destroy Palestinians amounts to accepting that Palestinians deserve to be treated as subhumans, as ‘<l1>human animals</l1>.’ Those are, after all, the words used by Israel’s Defence Minister, Yoav Gallant. Do the leaders of these Western governments think all this will have no consequences? Suppose Israel manages to destroy Hamas? And then what?”
Yacoub marque une pause, passe ses mains: Yacoub pauses, runs his hands over his face and starts up again, even more intensely. “What will we do with the new generation growing up in rage over what is being done to them, in the deep grief they live with every day? What will we do with these children who will have survived the ongoing <l1>ethnic cleansing</l1>? We are living through another Nakba right now, and not only in Gaza, but in the <l2>West Bank</l2> too!”
Pour Yacoub, « qu’on soit martyr, prison: For Yacoub, “whether you are a martyr, a prisoner or an exile, being Palestinian is an intifada, a revolt, a resistance.”
« Je vis cette guerre sur les écrans. Au: “I’m living this war on screens. As the days go by, my perception of things and my sensitivity have changed,” he says confidently. “I have to be stronger, for my family, for my people.”
Bien que son café ait refroidi, Yacoub c: Although his coffee has gone cold, Yacoub keeps sipping it. “My father always told me I must take care of my health, of my life, so I can keep carrying Palestine within me. But I hope that one day I’ll be able to live in a free Palestine, among the olive trees, on the shores of the Mediterranean. When we are free, I’ll invite you there for tea and a knafeh.”
Quelques jours après ma rencontre avec Y: A few days after I met Yacoub, the Awad family had to leave their shelter again under the bombing and walk about fifteen kilometres south in search of new refuge.
Depuis, Yacoub n’arrive plus à joindre s: Since then, Yacoub has been unable to reach his family and, as we publish this article, does not know where they are.
